ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: As shown in the figure, in $\triangle ABC$, $AB=AC$, $\angle BAC=120^\circ$, $AD\perp BC$ at $D$, $DE\perp AC$ at $E$. If $AE=3$, what is the length of $CE$?
ready1_open_rewrite.raw_answer_text:
\textbf{Solution:} Given: In $\triangle ABC$, $AB=AC$ and $\angle BAC=120^\circ$, \\
$\therefore$ $\angle B=\angle C=30^\circ$, \\
Since $AD\perp BC$ at $D$, \\
$\therefore$ $\angle ADC=90^\circ$, \\
$\therefore$ $\angle DAC=60^\circ$, \\
Since $DE\perp AC$, \\
$\therefore$ $\angle AED=90^\circ$, \\
$\therefore$ $\angle ADE=30^\circ$, \\
Given $AE=3$, \\
$\therefore$ $AD=2AE=6$, \\
$\therefore$ $AC=2AD=12$, \\
$\therefore$ $CE=AC-AE=\boxed{9}$.

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: In the figure is triangle ABC, B is on the left, C is on the right, BC is the base, and A is above; D is located on BC, AD connects downward from A to D, forming triangle ADC; E is located on side AC, DE connects from D to E, forming triangle ADE. The structure in the image is consistent with D being on BC, E being on AC, and the auxiliary triangles ADC and ADE in the problem statement. Then reason: From the problem statement AB=AC and ∠BAC=120°, triangle ABC is an isosceles triangle, so the base angles ∠B=∠C=(180°-120°)/2=30°. Because AD⊥BC, in triangle ADC, ∠ADC=90°, and also ∠C=30°, therefore ∠DAC=60°. Because DE⊥AC, triangle ADE is right-angled at E; and E is on AC, so ∠DAE=∠DAC=60°, hence ∠ADE=30°. In right triangle ADE, AE is the side opposite the 30° angle, and AD is the hypotenuse, so AD=2AE=2×3=6. In right triangle ADC, ∠C=30°, AD is the side opposite the 30° angle, and AC is the hypotenuse, so AC=2AD=12. Finally CE=AC-AE=12-3=9.
